newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.

text.p: South African Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals stopped the rand's rally dead in its tracks on Tuesday when he said its newfound strength could be a slight over-adjustment.
Speaking to Reuters shortly before a media briefing in Cape Town, Stals said: "I think there is a little bit of an over-adjustment but what is the right level of the rand?"

The comment touched of a wholesale exodus of dollars from the market which carved seven cents out of the rand as it weakened from a day's strongest level of 4.3790 bid against the U.S. unit shortly after 0800 GMT to 4.4530 at 1204 GMT.
"A lot of dollars left the market," a dealers said, adding that London players who had been selling dollars fairly heavily in the morning appeared to have been caught short.
"It seemed to gap...Stals was speaking and then suddenly it went much higher," he said.
The speed with which the currency moved prompted some traders to question Stals' timing of his comments.
One trader said the fact that most local players were on lunch when Stals' comments first hit the markets left the rand open to attack from offshore players.
"It was a thin lunchtime market and it was before lunch for the London and European guys and they had a go," he said.
Dealers said that the currency's pummelling drew support from the Reserve Bank as it sold dollars to major commercial banks.

"Yes, it (the central bank) has been selling dollars from all sorts of levels...from 4.41 upwards," a trader at one of South Africa's big four banks said when asked if the central bank had defended the rand.

Another trader said there was also talk that the Reserve Bank had sold dollars to banks before Stals' comments as part of a message to the markets that the current strength in financial markets may be a bit premature.
Central bank officials were not immediately available for comment.
Dealers said that while the market had turned, Stals' comments' were unlikely to do too much damage to sentiment.
They said that the rand could move to the 4.49 level in the short-term, before heading back to below the 4.40 level again.
"Its a bit overdone on the topside...in the longer-term we will come down (firm) again," one said, adding that Stals appeared to be signalling to the markets that recent gains might be premature.

The panic selling also reversed some of the rand's recent gains against the crosses. It was last quoted at 7.2832/2912 against sterling from 7.1766/1859 on Monday and at 0.3758/3726 marks from 0.3760/3764 previously.
The bond market, which had already reacted negatively to a sharply higher money market shortage, was also hit by heavy selling which pushed yields almost 30 points up from their intraday lows.
The key R150 was last quoted at 15.07 percent after trading between 15.85 percent and 15.12 percent on the day and from 14.91 percent overnight.

"We've seen an extremely adverse reaction to Stals' speech," said a senior bond trader. "It was not the kind of comment the market was looking for...we were looking for something a bit Traders said that foreigners in particular had ben heavy sellers on the day.
"When they saw Stals' speech they started dumping stock," the dealer said.
The market had already breached the 15.00 percent level earlier, however, after the central bank said the money market shortage jumped 2.4 billion rand to 10.275 billion rand on Monday.
Andre Kock, general manager of the Reserve Bank's money and capital markets said a mismatch in government flows was the main reason for the sharp rise in the shortage.
"There was a mismatch in government spending because some of the spending flowed through last week which normally would have flowed through over the weekend," Kock said.

The higher shortage had little impact on short-term rates, however, as three-month NCDs held steady at between 16.45 to 16.65 percent and the 90-day BA rate also remained unchanged at between 15.80 to 16.05 percent bid.

Bond Exchange figures showed foreigners bought a net 241.81 million rands worth of South African bonds on Monday after selling 432.00 million Friday, while nominal cumulative turnover was 8.67 billion rand on Monday from 7.08 billion rand on Friday.
-- Paul Richardson, Johannesburg newsroom, +27 11 482-1003
